title: Why MLX — Prince Canuma, Neywa Labs

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on serving models on-device via MLX, with quantization (Turbo Quant) and KV cache optimization as the key technical contribution. MLX is a general-purpose array framework for Apple Silicon that developers use to build and run AI applications locally without cloud dependency. The content focuses on deploying and serving pre-trained models on consumer Apple Silicon hardware. The talk assumes familiarity with ML frameworks and model serving but remains accessible through extensive live demonstrations. The presentation is a conference talk structured around live demos, framework overview, and community project showcases. summary: Prince Canuma opens by asking the audience about their experience running AI on phones and MacBooks, framing the talk around deploying AI agents fully on-device using MLX. His motivation is deeply personal: in 2020, his father lost his sight while Apple released powerful on-device chips. Living in Africa with unreliable internet, cloud-based solutions were inadequate, leading Canuma to conclude on-device AI is the future. He discovered MLX on GitHub in 2023—an array framework for Apple Silicon, comparable to PyTorch or TensorFlow—and began contributing. MLX now has over 1.5 million downloads, 4,000+ ported models, and day-zero support for frontier open-source models like Gemma 4. The talk progresses through vision capabilities (MLX VLM for real-time image analysis, powering LM Studio and Liquid AI), omni models that accept audio and image, and audio intelligence including Marvis (custom text-to-speech under 100ms), speech-to-text, and speech-to-speech with both Python and Swift support. A modular pipeline lets users chain ASR, language models, and TTS to fit any hardware budget. Live demos include real-time object detection with RFDetector, background blurring, and Gemma 4 local chat. Community projects include grounded visual reasoning for security and dashcam analysis, MLX video for on-device video generation on 16GB VRAM, a native voice app called Locally by Adrian using MLX audio and Marvis TTS, and a Richie Mini robot powered by MLX vision and audio with real-time Jarvis voice cloning. In Q&A, Canuma explains MLX uses the GPU not the neural engine (Core ML needed for neural engine, with hybrid inference coming), recommends Mactop for GPU monitoring, and suggests Gemma 4 e-versions and Qwen 3 Omni (~30B) as top omni models. He acknowledges current open-source models don't match Claude 3/4 Opus performance but expects parity in ~6 months. His Turbo Quant breakthrough, implemented 30 minutes after the paper's release, reduces KV cache by 4x with similar quality, enabling 1M context fully on device.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and motivation for on-device AI
sections.summary: Canuma opens by asking about audience experience running AI on devices, introduces the talk's goal of deploying AI agents on-device using MLX, and previews the agenda: why on-device, MLX framework, demos, and community projects.

sections.title: The origin story: Accessibility and Apple Silicon
sections.summary: In 2020, Canuma's father lost his sight while Apple released powerful on-device chips. Living in Africa with unreliable internet, cloud AI was impractical. Canuma promised his father he'd restore his ability to read, motivating his focus on on-device AI.

sections.title: Introduction to the MLX framework
sections.summary: Canuma discovered MLX on GitHub in 2023—an array framework for Apple Silicon like PyTorch or TensorFlow. He began contributing, and three years later MLX has 1.5M downloads, 4,000+ models, and day-zero support for frontier open-source models like Gemma 4.

sections.title: Vision capabilities: Empowering accessibility
sections.summary: MLX VLM gives vision capabilities for accessibility, originally prototyped as goggles at a hackathon, now on iPhone. It powers LM Studio and Liquid AI models. Large models with hundreds of billions of parameters can run on M1 MacBooks; Gemma 4 26B runs on iPhone.

sections.title: Audio intelligence: Controlling computers via voice
sections.summary: Canuma pursued audio for accessibility and personal productivity (Jarvis vision). Marvis generates audio in under 100ms. Speech-to-text enables voice control. Speech-to-speech with Python and Swift support allows native applications. Modular pipelines chain ASR, LLM, and TTS to fit any hardware budget.

sections.title: Vision demo: Real-time image analysis
sections.summary: Live demo of real-time object detection using RFDetector by Roboflow, running on-device with internet off. Detects a glass (identified as wine). Can also run on phone. Background blur demo shows real-time mask detection.

sections.title: Large language model demo: Running Gemma 4 locally
sections.summary: Demo of Gemma 4 via MLX VLM chat_ui with Gradio interface. Encountered technical difficulties with model downloading. Successfully analyzed a profile image, picking up details like name and bio. Demo machine has 96GB VRAM, enabling all showcased models to run simultaneously.

sections.title: Community projects: Grounded visual reasoning
sections.summary: Community project showing grounded visual reasoning: detecting fires and specific items in video, running on-device. Applications include security systems on MacBook and dashcam footage analysis.

sections.title: Video generation chains on-device
sections.summary: MLX video enables on-device video generation from text prompts. A user generated a cartoon by chaining multiple generations into a cohesive story rather than a single shot. Runs on 16GB VRAM MacBook.

sections.title: Native voice application showcase
sections.summary: Adrian, a participant, built an app called Locally using MLX audio and Marvis TTS, giving it the capability to speak back to users. Canuma plays a demo of the app narrating text with a strong voice, demonstrating beautiful native experiences possible with MLX.

sections.title: Robotics: Real-time voice cloning and interaction
sections.summary: Canuma shows his Richie Mini robot powered by MLX audio and MLX vision for perception via camera and audio input. The robot performs real-time voice cloning of the Iron Man Jarvis voice, responding to greetings. Canuma envisions building agents that can hear, see, and sound like humans on iPhone, iPad, Mac, or robots.

sections.title: Q&A: Neural engine usage and Core ML
sections.summary: Canuma explains MLX uses the GPU, not the neural engine. Enabling the neural engine requires Core ML, which currently doesn't provide an easy developer experience. He hopes WWDC will resolve private API issues, enabling hybrid inference across GPU and neural engine. He notes Apple may be integrating neural engine components into the GPU with M5 series.

sections.title: Q&A: Monitoring performance with Mactop
sections.summary: Canuma recommends Mactop (by Carson) for real-time GPU/CPU usage monitoring. He demonstrates launching inference with a 4-bit model while Mactop shows GPU usage increasing, providing an easy way to track performance.

sections.title: Q&A: Available model recommendations
sections.summary: For omni models, Canuma recommends Gemma 4 e-versions (e4, e2) which accept image, audio, and text, and Qwen 3 Omni at approximately 30 billion parameters, both runnable on-device.

sections.title: Q&A: Limitations and performance expectations
sections.summary: Canuma acknowledges current open-source models don't yet match Claude 3/4 Opus performance but expects parity in about 6 months. Otherwise, he sees no limitations: users can run inference on hundreds of images in parallel, process many documents, and achieve up to 1M context on device thanks to Turbo Quant.

sections.title: Q&A: Turbo Quant breakthrough and KV cache optimization
sections.summary: Canuma implemented Turbo Quant 30 minutes after the paper was published, and his tweet went viral with ~700K views. Turbo Quant reduces KV cache by 4x with similar quality (exact match to full model performance). At 300K context, throughput approximately doubles. This enables serving 1M context fully on-device depending on model size and hardware.
